_note: This episode is graded by DATED MILESTONES, not by a level series. No weekly or monthly container throughput series for the Port of Baltimore during the disruption could be obtained from any public source — see sources.json `_not_obtained`. Every milestone below is a dated fact read from a cited source; none is an estimate, and none required converting channel depth into a capacity percentage.
_turn_mapping_rule: Week 1 begins 2024-03-26 (the collapse). A dated milestone is assigned to the week index containing its date, counted in whole weeks from 2024-03-26.

milestones.note: 'the navigation channel was fully reopened, two and a half months after the event.' 11 June 2024 is 77 days after 26 March = week 11. This is the earliest date on which the PHYSICAL constraint on throughput was fully removed, so it is a lower bound on when capacity could have returned to normal — the model reaching baseline before this week is unambiguously too fast.

Commercial shipping was expected to return to normal levels in July 2024, with the port operating at normal capacity by mid-July — about week 16. RECORDED AS 'reported', NOT 'observed', because this is an expectation published on 2024-06-13 rather than a measured outcome, and it is therefore excluded from the scored count. It is retained because it bounds the plausible true recovery week from above.

_not_observed.reason: No weekly or monthly TEU series for the Port of Baltimore during March-August 2024 was obtainable publicly. Notably, the NEIGHBOURING ports' monthly volumes (NY/NJ, Virginia) were published promptly — observability is asymmetric, and the disrupted node is the hardest one to see.

No port-local transit-delay series exists. The global Sea-Intelligence series used for Yantian was deliberately NOT reused here: applying the same discredited global proxy to a second event would reproduce the first event's confounding rather than test the model independently.

Diverted volumes at NY/NJ (790,758 TEU in May 2024) and Virginia (>340,000 TEU in May 2024) were measured and published, but neither port authority quantified how much was Baltimore diversion, and the model's order_backlog is an index against a normal open order book that has no published counterpart.
No continuous public weekly lane rate series obtainable, as for Yantian.
Latent: firm-internal, no public counterpart attributable to this port.
Latent: firm-internal. The model's headline outcome remains unobservable in a second, entirely independent event — which is now a pattern rather than an accident of one case.
Operates at national/quarterly resolution; not attributable to one port inside a weekly window.
